title: Beyond florigen: role of FLOWERING LOCUS T1 on source-sink relation, reproduction, and vegetative development in barley
content: Reproductive and vegetative development are, together with longevity, crucial processes related to crop yield. In grasses like barley, the shoot apical meristem originates leaves during the vegetative growth (Wang et al. 2018) or spikelet meristems during reproductive growth (Bommert and Whipple 2018). This meristem identity and determinacy is controlled by the well-known florigen, the product of the gene FLOWERING LOCUS T1 (FT1) that, under proper flowering conditions, is expressed in leaves (Digel et al. 2015) and transported to a shoot apical meristem to start the transition to a spikelet meristem. Moreover, FT1 is known to be upregulated by PHOTOPERIOD 1 (Ppd-H1) (Shaw et al. 2013), stimulating flowering in the barley haplotype Golden Promise Fast (GP-Fast) (Digel et al. 2015) and delaying it when mutated in the Golden Promise cultivar (Jones et al. 2008). However, it remains unknown if Ppd-H1 has other targets than FT1 to control flowering. Also unknown are the identities of the downstream genes that interact with FT1 to regulate source (leaf)–sink (inflorescence) interactions for balanced vegetative and reproductive development. These questions have been addressed by Helmsorig and colleagues in this issue of Plant Physiology by creating CRISPR lines of ft1 in the haplotypes Golden Promise (ft1.1 and ft1.2, with mutated ppd-H1) and GP-Fast (ft1.3, with the wild-type allele of Ppd-H1).
